THE SESSION FLOW

One topic. A room of possibilities.

Why do companies such as Micron keep appearing in conversations about AI? This proposed session connects the hardware question to the work people want AI to do. We will trace a path from HBM and GPU infrastructure to Claude-based workflows, asking what limits a system at each layer and how to measure useful progress.

The session starts with a topical, speaker-led workshop. Then we will put the slides aside for exactly 15 minutes of pizza, casual conversation, and spontaneous discussion. Anyone who wants to keep going can stay for brainstorming, find potential teammates, and explore a research or startup idea. This is a technical and economic discussion, not a stock pitch or investment recommendation.

01 / SPEAKER-LED WORKSHOP

From the memory wall to useful work.

A topic speaker will guide the technical walkthrough, with space to pause, compare approaches, and work through examples. The speaker is to be confirmed; the outline and exercises below are proposed.

  1. 01

    Find the bottleneck: HBM & Micron

    The speaker will introduce memory capacity, bandwidth, and data movement, using HBM and Micron as a starting point. We will distinguish a workload that cannot fit in memory from one that spends too much time moving data.

    Suggested exercise: sketch the path from memory to accelerator and mark what you would measure before calling a workload compute-bound.

  2. 02

    Build the GPU infrastructure picture

    Move from a single accelerator to a usable system: interconnects, networking, power, cooling, scheduling, and utilization. The discussion will connect hardware choices to a concrete workload rather than treating GPU count as the goal.

    Suggested exercise: compare a single-GPU setup with a multi-GPU deployment and list the new bottlenecks each introduces.

  3. 03

    Evaluate a Claude-based workflow

    Move up the stack to a task with tools, inputs, and a testable result. The workshop will compare a predefined workflow with an agent-directed approach and discuss reliability, latency, review effort, and cost per successful task.

    Suggested exercise: outline a small evaluation set and a simple non-agent baseline before choosing a more complex system.

  4. 04

    Connect compute to productivity

    Bring the layers together: which constraint matters to the person using the result? We will discuss how completed, verified work differs from installed capacity, generated tokens, or a compelling demo.

    Suggested exercise: define a useful-work metric for one research or product workflow, including the human time needed to check the output.

02 / PIZZA & OPEN CONVERSATION

Put the slides aside.

15 MINUTES

After the workshop, we will take exactly 15 minutes for pizza, meeting new people, and free-form discussion. Join any conversation, compare notes with someone new, or bring up the question that did not fit into the workshop. There is no assigned group or required pitch.

Suggested conversation starters—not a record of questions asked:

  1. 01

    When is an AI workload limited by compute, memory bandwidth, memory capacity, or communication?

  2. 02

    What should a team measure before buying GPUs, renting capacity, or changing its deployment architecture?

  3. 03

    When does an agent add value over a simpler workflow—and how should we measure cost per successful task?

03 / OPTIONAL BRAINSTORMING & TEAM FORMATION

Stay for the idea you want to pursue.

The final segment is for anyone who wants to turn the conversation into a research question or startup idea. Bring an idea, join someone else’s, or listen first. Participation and team formation are optional—you do not need a finished pitch or a team in advance.

  • Find a shared question. Say what interests you, who a solution might help, and what you would like to learn.
  • Meet possible teammates. Compare interests and skills, then decide whether you want to explore an idea together.
  • Choose a first test. Sketch a small experiment or prototype, the evidence it should produce, and what support the team might need.

Possible starting points

These are suggested project directions, not existing teams, announced projects, or reported outcomes.

  • Research direction

    A bottleneck field guide

    Design a reproducible comparison that records memory use, data movement, utilization, and end-to-end task time across a small set of workloads.

  • Research / startup direction

    A workflow evaluation bench

    Compare a simple baseline and a Claude-based workflow on one narrow task, tracking verified completion, review effort, latency, and cost.

  • Startup direction

    Useful-compute planning for small teams

    Explore a tool that helps a team describe its workload, identify likely constraints, and test deployment choices before expanding its infrastructure.

AFTER THE SESSION / SUPPORT & FOLLOW-UP

An idea can keep going after the room clears.

Teams can discuss available PCPU support and agree on next steps. Resource support will depend on the project’s needs and what the organization can make available; this is not a promise of funding, equipment, or a fixed allocation.

PCPU will stay in touch with teams that choose to continue. Follow-up check-ins will give teams a place to share progress, surface blockers, and refine their next experiment or prototype. The check-in plan and any resource arrangements will be agreed with each team.

A PROMPT TO TAKE WITH YOU

What would demonstrate that AI compute is becoming productive infrastructure rather than merely installed capacity?
